nodes.label: Sidon early dominance
nodes.full: Sidon emerged as the leading Phoenician city in the centuries immediately after the Bronze Age Collapse, prosperous enough that Homer's epics use 'Sidonian' as a generic term for fine Phoenician craftsmanship generally — a dominance Tyre would only gradually eclipse over the following two centuries.
nodes.src: Homer, Iliad and Odyssey, using 'Sidonian' generically for Phoenician luxury goods.

nodes.label: Hiram I and Tyre
nodes.full: Hiram I expanded Tyre's harbours and territory, formed a documented alliance and trade partnership with Israel's kings David and Solomon supplying cedar timber and craftsmen for the Jerusalem Temple's construction, and established Tyre as the dominant Phoenician power for the following centuries.
nodes.src: 1 Kings 5:1–12 and 9:10–14, on Hiram's alliance with Solomon; Josephus, Against Apion 1.17–18, citing Tyrian royal annals.

nodes.label: Cedar timber trade
nodes.full: Lebanon's cedar forests supplied timber to Egypt and Mesopotamia for millennia before this period and continued to do so throughout it — Solomon's Temple construction, financed partly by grain and oil in exchange for Hiram's cedar and craftsmen, is only the best-documented single instance of a trade relationship stretching back to the Old Kingdom Egyptian texts describing Byblos as a timber source.
nodes.src: 1 Kings 5:6–11, on the cedar-for-provisions exchange with Hiram of Tyre; comparative ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian textual references to Lebanese cedar imports.

nodes.label: Melqart of Tyre
nodes.full: Melqart, Tyre's patron god associated with kingship, the sea and the city's own founding, was worshipped at a temple Herodotus himself reported visiting and marvelling at — Greek visitors would later identify Melqart with Herakles, a syncretism that carried the god's cult, under a new name, to Phoenician colonies across the Mediterranean including Cadiz's own famous Melqart-Herakles temple.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 2.44, describing the Tyrian temple of Melqart/Herakles.

nodes.label: King and council
nodes.full: Phoenician cities combined hereditary kingship with a council of leading merchant families whose consent mattered for major decisions — a mixed constitutional model later transplanted to Carthage, where the council eventually eclipsed kingship entirely, showing an institutional lineage running from the Phoenician homeland to its most successful colonial offshoot.
nodes.src: Comparative evidence for Phoenician civic institutions from Tyrian and Carthaginian sources; Aristotle, Politics 2.11, on the Carthaginian constitution's Phoenician roots.

nodes.label: Assyrian and Babylonian overlordship
nodes.full: Successive Assyrian and then Neo-Babylonian empires reduced the Phoenician cities to tribute-paying vassals, tolerating local kingship and considerable commercial autonomy so long as tribute was paid — Tyre's island location let it survive as a going concern through repeated sieges that mainland Sidon could not withstand in the same way.
nodes.src: Assyrian royal annals (Shalmaneser III, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) on Phoenician tribute and vassalage.

nodes.label: Shalmaneser III imposes tribute
nodes.full: The bronze relief bands from the gates of Balawat depict Tyrian and Sidonian tribute-bearers presenting goods to the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III — visual and textual confirmation that Phoenician cities were paying regular tribute to Assyria from at least the mid-9th century BC, decades before the more famous later Assyrian campaigns against the coast.
nodes.src: Balawat Gates bronze bands, British Museum, depicting Shalmaneser III's Phoenician tribute.

nodes.label: Esarhaddon destroys Sidon
nodes.full: After Sidon's king Abdi-Milkutti rebelled and sought Egyptian support, the Assyrian king Esarhaddon besieged and razed the city, beheaded the king, deported much of the population, and built a new Assyrian administrative city on the site — a fate Tyre, protected by its island position, would avoid for another century.
nodes.src: Esarhaddon's annals (the Sidon inscription), on the destruction of Sidon.

nodes.label: Siege of Tyre
nodes.full: The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II besieged island Tyre for thirteen years without ever fully conquering it by force, eventually reaching a negotiated settlement that left Tyre's monarchy intact but firmly subordinate — a siege whose sheer length testifies to how effectively Tyre's island fortifications and naval resources could resist even a major imperial army.
nodes.src: Ezekiel 29:18, referencing the siege's inconclusive outcome; Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, citing Tyrian records on the siege's length and settlement.

nodes.label: Squeezed between empires
nodes.full: Phoenicia's small, wealthy coastal city-states never developed a unified territorial state or standing army capable of matching Assyria, Babylon or Egypt, instead surviving for centuries through a combination of tribute payment, diplomatic flexibility and, in Tyre's case, defensible island geography — commercial wealth substituting for the military power its city-states individually and collectively lacked.
nodes.src: Comparative political-geographic analysis of Phoenician city-state survival strategies under successive imperial overlordship.

nodes.label: Murex purple industry
nodes.full: Producing Tyrian purple required crushing tens of thousands of murex sea snails to yield even small quantities of dye, an industry whose enormous discarded shell middens still mark the ancient dye works along the Phoenician coast — one of the most labour-intensive luxury manufacturing processes documented anywhere in the ancient world.
nodes.src: Murex shell midden archaeological surveys, Tyre and Sidon coastal sites.

nodes.label: Prestige of Tyrian purple
nodes.full: Dye extracted in minute, labour-intensive quantities from the glands of murex sea snails produced a colourfast purple so costly that it became associated exclusively with royalty and high status across the ancient Mediterranean world — the very word 'Phoenician' likely derives from a Greek term connected to this purple, making the dye industry central to the culture's own name in other languages.
nodes.src: Comparative ancient Mediterranean textual and archaeological evidence for Tyrian purple production and cost.

nodes.label: Shipbuilding
nodes.full: Phoenician shipwrights built both deep-hulled round merchant vessels for bulk cargo and narrower galleys for speed and, eventually, ramming warfare — maritime engineering sophisticated enough that later Mediterranean naval powers, including the Greeks, Assyrians and eventually Rome, drew directly on Phoenician ship design and, in Assyria's own case, Phoenician crews.
nodes.src: Assyrian palace reliefs depicting Phoenician-built and Phoenician-crewed ships in Assyrian service; comparative ancient Mediterranean shipbuilding evidence.

nodes.label: Glassmaking
nodes.full: Pliny the Elder's famous story of Phoenician merchants accidentally inventing glass by propping cooking pots on natron blocks on a Levantine beach is almost certainly a folk legend rather than a literal historical account, since glass technology considerably predates the Phoenicians — but Phoenician workshops, especially at Sidon, did become major glass producers and exporters by the later part of this period regardless of the technology's actual origin.
nodes.src: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 36.65, the glassmaking-origin legend, flagged as legendary rather than a reliable historical account.

nodes.label: Ivory carving
nodes.full: Carved ivory furniture inlays and decorative plaques produced by Phoenician workshops were exported and treasured as luxury goods as far as the Assyrian palaces at Nimrud, where excavators recovered enormous quantities of them, and later into Greek and Etruscan elite contexts — a Phoenician decorative style distinguishable from contemporary Egyptian and Syrian ivory carving by its own hybrid Egyptianising motifs.
nodes.src: Nimrud ivories, British Museum; Max Mallowan excavations, Nimrud (1949–63 seasons).

nodes.label: Alphabet standardized
nodes.full: Phoenician scribes standardised a 22-consonant alphabetic script — visible in dated royal inscriptions like the Ahiram sarcophagus from Byblos — that Phoenician traders then carried across the Mediterranean; Greek tradition itself credited a Phoenician, Cadmus, with introducing the alphabet, and the Greek alphabet's own letter names and order closely track the Phoenician original.
nodes.src: Ahiram sarcophagus inscription, Byblos, National Museum of Beirut; Herodotus, Histories 5.58, on the Phoenician origin of the Greek alphabet.

nodes.label: Alphabet reaches Greece
nodes.full: Phoenician merchants and settlers, documented archaeologically at Cyprus's Kition and elsewhere in the Aegean, transmitted their alphabetic script to Greek speakers who adapted it by adding vowel letters — a single act of cultural transmission whose descendant scripts, Greek and Latin, would go on to be used for a large share of the world's writing systems ever since.
nodes.src: Comparative Phoenician-Greek epigraphic evidence for the alphabet's transmission, 9th–8th century BC Aegean contexts.

nodes.label: Founding of Carthage
nodes.full: Tradition credits Tyrian exiles led by a princess later Roman sources called Dido with founding Carthage on the North African coast in 814 BC — whatever the founding legend's precise historicity, Carthage grew within a few centuries into Phoenicia's most powerful and enduring colonial daughter-city, eventually eclipsing Tyre itself in wealth and military reach.
nodes.src: Timaeus of Tauromenium (via later citations) and Justin's Epitome of Pompeius Trogus, on Carthage's traditional founding date and Dido legend.

nodes.label: Mediterranean maritime network
nodes.full: Phoenician trading posts and colonies stretching from the Levantine coast through Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa to Cadiz on the Atlantic made Phoenicia's cities, individually militarily modest, collectively the organisers of the ancient Mediterranean's first genuinely basin-wide commercial network, centuries before Greek or Roman maritime power matched its reach.
nodes.src: Comparative archaeological distribution mapping of Phoenician colonial and trading-post sites across the Mediterranean.

nodes.label: Phoenician traders as slavers
nodes.full: Homer's Odyssey describes Phoenician traders as skilled merchants who were also opportunistic kidnappers, luring or seizing individuals to sell into slavery elsewhere in the Mediterranean — a documented reputation, whatever its degree of literary exaggeration, for a trading network whose commercial success rested in part on trafficking in human beings alongside legitimate goods.
nodes.src: Homer, Odyssey 14.287–297, 15.415–484, on Phoenician traders and slave-taking.

nodes.label: Disputed child sacrifice
nodes.full: Greek and Roman writers accused Phoenicians and especially Carthaginians of routinely sacrificing children to Baal Hammon and Tanit, and archaeologists have excavated infant burial precincts (tophets) at several Punic sites — but whether these represent actual ritual killing, high infant-mortality burial of the already-dead, or some combination remains a genuinely unresolved and actively debated question rather than settled fact in either direction.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 20.14, the fullest ancient literary accusation; ongoing archaeological and osteological debate over the Carthage tophet's interpretation.

nodes.label: Tophet evidence
nodes.full: Osteological analysis of infant and child cremated remains from Punic tophet precincts shows a mixed age profile including some very young infants and some older children, evidence researchers read in sharply different ways — as consistent with a mix of natural infant mortality and possible sacrifice, or as supporting the ancient literary accusations more directly — a genuinely open question the skeletal evidence alone has not settled.
nodes.src: Comparative osteological and demographic analysis of Punic tophet infant burial age profiles, various published studies with differing conclusions.

nodes.label: Bronze Age collapse
nodes.full: The Late Bronze Age collapse destroyed the Levantine city-states and left the coastal Phoenician cities to emerge from the wreckage.
nodes.src: background — see the Canaan 2000–1200 BC folio
